lecture.script:
Good morning. Today we look at vertical farming: growing food in stacked layers inside buildings, under electric light, in the middle of a city. It sounds futuristic, but the first commercial farms of this kind opened only about fifteen years ago.

Start with a simple question: where does a city's salad come from? In most cities, lettuce is trucked in from farms hundreds of kilometres away. That journey costs money and the leaves lose freshness before they reach the shelf. Farming closer to the city sounds obvious, but around most large cities there is very little land left.

Vertical farms answer this by moving indoors. Because the building controls temperature and light, the season outside stops mattering, and you can harvest lettuce in January in a cold climate. Many of these farms occupy abandoned warehouses, which are cheap and already wired for electricity.

The water story surprises people. In an open field, most of the water you apply sinks into the soil or evaporates. In a closed indoor system, the same water goes around the system again and again, so one of these farms can use ninety per cent less water than a field growing the identical crop.

Space works differently too. A field can only get bigger sideways. Indoors, when you want more growing area, you stack another layer on top rather than buy another field, so ten layers in one building equal ten fields of surface. The difficulty is electricity. Lighting is the single largest cost, and researchers are still testing which crops earn that cost back. Leafy greens do. Wheat, so far, does not.

lecture.script:
Good afternoon. Tonight, while you sleep, your brain will be busy sorting through everything that happened today. Let me explain what we now know about sleep and memory.

For most of the twentieth century, sleep was treated as a kind of switching off. Textbooks described the sleeping brain as idle, simply waiting for morning. Students were told that if they wanted to remember something, the answer was more hours of study, and sleep was time taken away from that study.

The picture changed in the nineteen nineties, when researchers began recording brain activity through the night. They found that the patterns produced while an animal learned a maze during the day were played again during sleep, faster and in the same order. Nothing was switching off at all.

We now think of sleep as the stage where a memory becomes permanent. During the day, new information is held in a small structure near the centre of the brain. At night, the same information is copied out to the outer surface, where it can last for years. Wake someone repeatedly during the deepest stage of sleep, and the copying never finishes.

There is a second effect, and it is easier to demonstrate. Give two groups a list of word pairs. Let one group sleep for eight hours and keep the other awake for the same eight hours. Test them the next evening, when both are equally tired. The group that slept remembers about forty per cent more. So sleep is not a gap in learning. It is part of the process, and it cannot be replaced by extra hours at the desk.

lecture.script:
Hello everyone. When you picture plastic in the ocean, you probably picture a beach. Today I want to move your attention upstream, to rivers.

For twenty years, ocean clean-up campaigns focused almost entirely on the shoreline. Volunteers walked beaches with bags, and the photographs were powerful. But once plastic reaches open water, it breaks into pieces smaller than a grain of rice, and at that size no net can pick it up. Removing it out there costs roughly a hundred times what it costs to stop it on land.

That is why attention has shifted to rivers. A recent survey traced the plastic entering the sea and found something unexpected: a very small number of rivers carry the great majority of it. Just over a thousand rivers, out of about a hundred thousand worldwide, account for eighty per cent of the plastic reaching the ocean. Almost all of these are short rivers running through dense cities where waste collection has not kept pace with population growth.

This changes what a solution looks like. Instead of one global campaign, you can place barriers at a small number of specific points, because a floating barrier across a river mouth catches material while it is still large enough to grab.

But I want to be careful here. Barriers treat the symptom. The plastic still has to be paid for by someone, and in many of these cities the real gap is that rubbish is never picked up in the first place. A barrier is also useless during floods, when it must be opened. So the honest summary is this: rivers give us a cheaper place to act, not a complete answer.

lecture.script:
Good morning. Today's topic is the bicycle sharing system, and I want to use it to show you how a small design decision can decide whether a public service works.

The first generation appeared in Amsterdam in nineteen sixty-five. White bicycles were left unlocked around the city for anyone to use. The idea was beautiful and it collapsed within a month, because almost every bicycle was stolen or thrown into a canal. For thirty years afterwards, city governments treated the whole concept as impossible.

The second generation added coin locks, but it did not fix the deeper problem. Nobody knew who had taken a bicycle, so nobody was answerable for it. What changed everything in the two thousands was not the bicycle. It was the card reader. Once each trip is linked to a named account, the bicycle stops being anonymous, and losses fall to a level a city can live with.

That brings us to today's numbers. In the largest systems, each bicycle is now used between four and eight times a day. Compare that with a privately owned bicycle, which sits unused for more than twenty-three hours out of twenty-four. The same piece of metal serves many more people.

And yet these systems rarely pay for themselves. Riders' fees typically cover about fifty per cent of the running cost. The heaviest expense is not repair. It is trucks, moving bicycles back uphill and out of the centre every night, because riders take them downhill in the morning and leave them there. Some cities now pay riders a small credit for returning a bicycle to an empty station, which is cheaper than sending a truck.

lecture.script:
Good morning. About one bite in three of the food on your plate exists because an insect visited a flower. Today I want to look at who those insects actually are.

When people talk about pollination, they usually mean one species: the honeybee. Honeybees are easy to keep, easy to move, and a single hive holds tens of thousands of workers. So for decades, growers of almonds, apples and blueberries have solved pollination by renting hives, trucking them in when the flowers open and taking them away afterwards.

That approach has been under pressure since two thousand six, when beekeepers in North America began losing around a third of their hives each winter. The causes are still argued about, but the effect on growers is simple. The price of renting a hive has roughly tripled in twenty years.

Here is the part that surprises people. Honeybees are not always the best pollinators. A honeybee packs pollen tightly onto its legs to carry it home, which means less of it rubs off on the next flower. A bumblebee is messier, and messier is better. Bumblebees also work in cool, wet weather that keeps honeybees inside the hive.

And wild insects are already doing far more than growers assume. Careful counts in orchards show that wild bees and flies, arriving with no rent to pay, carry out roughly half the pollination even in fields where hives have been placed. Those insects need hedges and rough ground near the orchard. A farm that removes every hedge to gain a little planting area is quietly paying for something it used to get free.

lecture.script:
Good afternoon. Twenty years ago, a common prediction was that public libraries would close. The internet had arrived, everything was going online, and a building full of paper looked like a museum. That prediction turned out to be wrong, and the reason it was wrong is instructive.

Let me describe the old model first. A library was defined by what it held. Success was measured by the number of volumes on the shelves and the number of items borrowed each year. Staff spent much of their day at a desk, stamping cards and answering questions about where a book was located. The visitor's purpose was assumed: you came in, you took something away, you left.

Both of those measures did fall. In most countries, book lending peaked in the late nineteen nineties and has declined every year since. If holdings and loans were the only test, the prediction would have been right.

But visits did not fall with them. In many cities, the number of people walking through the door has risen, and what those people are doing inside has changed completely. They are using free internet access, sitting in a warm room, taking a language class, printing a job application, or letting a child attend a reading hour. In one large system, two thirds of visitors last year borrowed nothing at all.

So the library has quietly become something else: not a store of books, but a place a city provides where you are not required to buy anything. That is harder to count than loans, which is precisely the problem. When budgets are cut, the number that gets shown to politicians is still the number of loans, and by that number every library looks like it is failing.

lecture.script:
Good morning. Electric cars are often discussed as a battery problem. I want to argue that the harder problem is where the electricity is delivered.

Start with the battery. In two thousand ten, a battery pack cost around one thousand one hundred dollars per kilowatt hour. Today it is under a hundred and forty. That is one of the fastest cost reductions in industrial history, and an electric car and a petrol car now cost roughly the same to build.

So why has adoption been so patchy? Survey after survey gives the same answer, and it is not price. Buyers say they are afraid of running out of charge on a long journey. Notice, though, that this fear does not match how people actually drive. The average daily distance in most countries is under fifty kilometres, well within any modern car's range. What buyers are really telling us is that they do not trust the network of charging points, not that they need a bigger battery.

And the numbers support them. Where those chargers sit is another matter. In several European countries there is one charger for every ten electric cars; in others the figure is one for every forty. Worse, roughly one in five public chargers is out of order at any moment, and a driver cannot know before arriving.

Which points to the real lesson. Home charging solves this for anyone with a driveway, and about eighty per cent of charging already happens overnight at home. But in cities, most people park on the street, and for them no driveway means no overnight charging. So the group least able to charge conveniently is the urban population, exactly the group cities most want to move out of petrol cars.

lecture.script:
Good morning. Today's story is about the simplest medical intervention ever discovered, and about how long it took to be accepted.

Vienna, eighteen forty-seven. A young doctor named Semmelweis worked in a hospital with two maternity wards. In the first ward, staffed by doctors, about one mother in ten died after giving birth. In the second, staffed by midwives, the figure was closer to one in thirty. The wards took women on alternate days, so the patients were not different. Something about the first ward was killing them.

Semmelweis noticed that the doctors, unlike the midwives, came straight from performing autopsies. He could not explain why that mattered, because nobody yet knew that microbes existed. But he insisted that every doctor rinse his hands in a chlorine solution before entering the ward. Deaths in the first ward fell to the level of the second within a year.

And here is the uncomfortable part. His colleagues rejected him. Some were insulted by the suggestion that a gentleman's hands could be dirty. Others pointed out, correctly, that he had no theory to explain the result. Semmelweis was eventually dismissed from the hospital, and hand washing was not general practice for another forty years, until Pasteur's work made the mechanism clear.

The modern lesson is not just historical. Studies in today's hospitals find that staff clean their hands on well under half the occasions when guidelines require it. And the reason given is almost never disagreement. It is time. A nurse on a busy ward may have dozens of such occasions in an hour, and the sink is not always close by. So the barrier has moved from belief to design.

lecture.script:
Good afternoon. Roughly a third of the food grown in the world is never eaten. Today I want to be precise about where in the chain that food is lost, because the answer decides what you should do about it.

There is a common assumption that waste is mainly a consumer failure: shoppers buying too much and throwing it away. Public campaigns have followed this assumption for years, with posters about planning your meals and checking your fridge.

But the picture depends entirely on which country you look at. In low income countries, most of the loss happens before the food ever reaches a shop. Grain sits in the open and gets wet before anyone can store it. Vegetables travel for days in unrefrigerated trucks on poor roads, and much of a harvest can be gone by the time it arrives. There, food never reaches consumers at all, so consumer advice is beside the point.

In high income countries the pattern inverts. Storage and transport are good, and the largest single share is lost in kitchens, both household and restaurant. So the same global figure hides two completely different problems requiring two different remedies.

One further point, and it is the one people find least intuitive. Not all waste weighs the same environmentally. A kilogram of beef thrown away represents around sixty times the greenhouse emissions of a kilogram of potatoes, because of everything that went into producing it. So a campaign that reduces the total weight of waste may achieve very little, while a campaign focused narrowly on meat and dairy could achieve a great deal. Weight is the easy thing to measure. It is not the thing that matters.

lecture.script:
Good morning. There are about seven thousand languages spoken today, and by the end of this century linguists expect roughly half of them to have no speakers left. I want to look at how that happens, and at what the standard response gets wrong.

First, how a language ends. It is almost never sudden. The usual pattern takes three generations. Grandparents speak the local language at home. Parents understand it but answer their own children in the national language, because that is the language of school and work. The grandchildren can follow a conversation but cannot produce a sentence. Nothing is banned and nobody decides. Each family simply makes a reasonable choice, and the sum of those choices ends a language.

Second, what linguists do about it. For most of the twentieth century, the response was documentation. Send a researcher, record the last fluent speakers, write a grammar and a dictionary, and place them in a university archive. The tapes are safe. Nobody listens to them.

And this is where I want to be blunt. A recorded language is not a living one. A grammar in an archive lets a scholar study a language; it does not let a child grow up in it. If the goal is speakers rather than data, the work has to happen where families make daily decisions.

There is one encouraging case. Hebrew had no native speakers for centuries and now has millions. But look at what it required: a state, a school system, and an army all operating in the language. No archive did that. Which means archives are worth keeping, but nobody should mistake them for a rescue.

lecture.script:
Good morning. On a summer afternoon, the centre of a large city can be seven degrees warmer than the farmland outside it. That gap has a name, the urban heat island, and today I want to explain both why it exists and why the obvious remedy is more complicated than it looks.

The cause is mostly material. Asphalt and dark roofing absorb sunlight all day and give it back little by little all through the night, so a city never fully cools down before the next morning. Add the heat thrown out by air conditioners and engines, and you have a surface that stays warm around the clock.

Now, trees. A mature street tree does two things at once. Its canopy blocks sunlight before it reaches the pavement, and it releases water vapour from its leaves, which draws heat out of the air just as sweating does. Measurements under a good canopy show temperatures several degrees below the open street a few metres away.

But here is the difficulty. Cooling depends on canopy area, and canopy area takes decades. A tree planted this spring will provide almost no shade for fifteen years, and roughly a third of newly planted street trees die within five, usually from lack of water in their first two summers. And the trees are not distributed evenly. In city after city, wealthy districts have two to three times the canopy of poor ones. The neighbourhoods with the least shade also tend to have the smallest homes and the fewest air conditioners. So the heat falls hardest on the people least equipped to escape it.

lecture.script:
Good morning. You paid something like four dollars for a cup of coffee this morning. Today I want to follow that four dollars backwards, from your hand to the farm, because the shape of the answer tells you a lot about international trade.

Of your four dollars, the farmer who grew the beans receives somewhere between three and ten cents. The rest is divided among shipping, roasting, packaging, the shop's rent, and the wages of the person who served you. This is not a story of one greedy company. It is the ordinary arithmetic of a long chain.

Why so little at the farm end? Because the farmer sells the cheapest version of the product. Green coffee, unroasted, is a commodity. Any sack is interchangeable with any other sack of the same grade, so the price is set on a world exchange and no individual grower can influence it. Meanwhile, the roasted, branded, ground coffee in your cup is not interchangeable at all, and whoever owns that stage sets their own price.

So the interesting question is where along the chain value gets added. And notice what that implies. If a producing country roasts and packages its own coffee, it captures far more of the final price. Ethiopia has been trying exactly this for two decades.

But it is harder than it sounds. Roasted coffee goes stale within weeks, so shipping it means air freight or refrigeration. Importing countries also charge a far heavier duty on roasted coffee than on green beans, which quietly discourages the very step that would help. And building recognised brands abroad takes money that a small grower simply does not have.

lecture.script:
Good afternoon. Today's subject is attention, and I want to start by narrowing the question. The popular claim is that phones have shortened our attention spans permanently. That claim is much weaker than the evidence for something more specific and more interesting.

Begin with the well-established part. Switching between two tasks carries a cost. When you move from writing an essay to reading a message and back again, you do not resume where you left off. Part of your mind stays on the message, and studies put the recovery time at up to twenty minutes for demanding work. Over a day of frequent switching, that adds up to hours of reduced capacity.

Now the finding that surprised researchers. In one series of experiments, students sat a test with their phone either in another room, in a bag, or face down on the desk. The phone was silent in all three conditions. Scores were highest with the phone in another room and lowest with it on the desk, even though nobody in that group reported feeling distracted. The device did not have to do anything. Its presence was enough, because part of the mind was occupied with not looking at it.

So the important claim is not about damage. It is about location. And notice the practical consequence: turning off notifications is a smaller intervention than most people assume, because the effect measured here was produced by a silent phone.

One caution before we finish. These effects are averages, and the size varies a great deal between individuals. And permanent change in the brain is not what has been shown. Move the phone to another room and the capacity comes back the same afternoon.

lecture.script:
Good morning. Most of you sorted your rubbish this week and felt you had done something useful. Today I want to look at what actually happens to it, and I should warn you that the picture is not flattering.

Begin with the numbers for plastic. Globally, about nine per cent of all plastic ever produced has been recycled. Twelve per cent has been burned. The remaining seventy-nine per cent is in landfill or in the environment. Note that this is a figure for the whole history of plastic, not for one bad year.

Why so low, when collection rates in many countries are high? The problem is that collection and recycling are different things. A household may sort perfectly, and the material may still be turned away further down the line. Some is contaminated with food. Some is a mixture of layers that no process can separate. And some has simply been produced in a form nobody has built a market for.

This is where the design of the product decides everything. A clear drinks bottle made of a single material can be turned back into a bottle many times. A pouch made of plastic film bonded to a metal layer cannot be pulled apart economically by any known method, no matter how carefully it is sorted.

So the decisive moment for a package is not the moment you put it in a bin. It is the moment an engineer chose its materials, years earlier and hundreds of kilometres away. Which suggests where regulation should point. Several countries now charge producers a fee that rises with how hard their packaging is to process, and that fee, unlike a public campaign, changes what gets designed.

lecture.script:
Good afternoon. Most people know that city lights are bad for migrating birds. Rather fewer can say why, and the why turns out to matter a great deal for what we should do about it.

Start with the scale. In North America, collisions with buildings kill somewhere between a hundred million and a billion birds a year. The range is wide because the counting is hard, but even the low figure is very large. And here is the first point that surprises people: the great majority of the birds involved are travelling at night.

Now the mechanism. These birds steer partly by the pattern of the stars. A brightly lit tower breaks that pattern. The birds lose the sky they were reading, circle the light for hours, and arrive at dawn exhausted in the middle of a city. Then they meet the glass, which is reflective and shows them trees and open air that are not there. So the glass is the last step in a chain, not the beginning of it.

One large building in Chicago gave us a natural experiment. Its window bays were sometimes lit and sometimes dark, depending on the events held inside. Across twenty-one years of records, on nights when half the bays were dark, collisions fell to roughly one sixth of the number counted on fully lit nights. Weather explained a little of that difference, but nowhere near all of it.

One caution before we stop. The birds do not pass evenly. Concentrate on the two or three weeks in spring and autumn when most of them move, and a lights-out rule buys almost the whole benefit for very little cost. Chicago's rule is voluntary, and that, not its design, is its weakness.
